summary:
The bill establishes a new regulatory framework for online platforms regarding minors' safety and privacy, amending multiple federal statutes. Its operative mechanism imposes duties of care, safeguard requirements, and transparency mandates on "covered platforms" while significantly expanding the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (COPPA).

Title I, Subtitle A (Kids Online Safety) creates new obligations for "covered platforms" (defined in Sec. 101 with specific exceptions, including common carriers, broadband services, email, and certain non-profits). Section 102 imposes a duty to exercise reasonable care in creating and implementing design features to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors (individuals under 17), including mental health disorders, addiction-like behaviors, and sexual exploitation. Section 103 mandates that covered platforms provide minors with readily-accessible safeguards to limit communications, restrict personal data visibility, control personalized recommendation systems, and restrict geolocation sharing. Default settings for users known to be minors must be set to the most protective level. Parental tools are required, with default enablement for users known to be children (under 13). Section 104 requires clear, conspicuous notice of policies and safeguards, including verifiable parental consent for children before initial use. Section 105 requires annual public reports based on independent, third-party audits for platforms with over 10,000,000 monthly active U.S. users that predominantly provide a community forum for user-generated content; the report must assess reasonably foreseeable risks of harms to minors. Section 108 directs a study on device-level age verification. Section 110 treats violations as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act and authorizes State Attorneys General to bring civil actions for violations of Sections 103, 104, or 105. Section 111 establishes a Kids Online Safety Council not subject to FACA. The effective date is 18 months after enactment (Sec. 112). Section 130 preempts conflicting state laws but explicitly permits states to enact greater protections for minors.

Subtitle B (Filter Bubble Transparency) makes it unlawful, one year after enactment, to operate an online platform using an "opaque algorithm" (defined in Sec. 120) unless the platform provides notice and enables users to switch to an "input-transparent algorithm." Violations are enforced under the FTC Act.

Title II amends COPPA. Section 201 amends 15 U.S.C. §§ 6501-6505 to: expand the definition of "operator"; redefine "personal information" to include additional identifiers, biometric data, and geolocation; add the term "teen" (ages 13-16); prohibit personal information collection for individual-specific advertising to children and teens; require verifiable consent from teens; establish new rights for parents and teens to delete or correct personal information; and impose data retention limits. The amendments also address educational operator agreements, require an FTC feasibility assessment of a common verifiable consent mechanism, and add a preemption clause mirroring Title I. Section 202 mandates annual FTC enforcement reports and a study on mobile application oversight. Section 203 requires a GAO study on teens' use of financial technology products.

Title III amends 31 U.S.C. § 1125 and 31 U.S.C. § 1105(a) to require agency heads to include in budget justification materials a list of recurring plans or reports, identify those that are outdated or duplicative, and recommend sunsetting, modification, consolidation, or frequency reduction. It also amends Section 7244 of the FY2023 NDAA to conform report submission requirements.
